prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube first because I weigh detector development leading to discovery heavily, but after reading all eight ballots I move optical lattice clocks to the top. B005 is the only shortlisted candidate that seven of eight members place in their top three, and the reasons are scientific, not just a count: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the light-shift problem, and Ye's group took the clocks to roughly 1e-18 systematic uncertainty. Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) reproduce this performance and compare clocks across fibre links. That is exactly the independent confirmation I look for, and as an instrument builder I recognise the calibration and systematics effort behind it. The physics will last, with applications to tests of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches and relativistic geodesy, and it fits a two-person, cleanly attributed prize.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap and scope: the 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch, frequency comb) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, ion control) already honoured neighbouring precision-metrology work, so the committee must be able to state what is new in the lattice clock. There is also a priority question about single-ion optical clocks and parallel lattice proposals, and contributors such as Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley fall outside the two-name credit. Finally, atomic physics is outside my own expertise, and I am relying on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson to confirm that Katori and Ye are the decisive pair.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B005 first, notes that Katori invented the magic-wavelength concept and Ye drove the record implementations, but asks whether the prize should be tied to the clock invention or to the wider comb and metrology lineage already honoured in 2005.
responses.response: I agree with the narrow framing and would keep the citation on the lattice clock itself. The 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a ruler. The lattice clock is a different step, with many atoms interrogated in a Lamb-Dicke regime at the magic wavelength, and it reached stability and accuracy that single-ion and microwave clocks cannot match. I would accept this only if the citation avoids any suggestion that it re-rewards the comb. I also thank Danielsson for ranking IceCube second; I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B035 sixth because neutrino astronomy is young, source identification is limited to a few objects, and attribution inside a roughly 300-person collaboration makes a trio an unusual simplification.
responses.response: This is a fair challenge and it moves me off my opening first place. I still think the diffuse-flux observation is solid, since it is seen in several channels and independent analyses, but the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 identifications have moderate significance and the source population is open. I disagree with her on the length of the wait, because the 2013 discovery is now well over a decade old, but I accept that IceCube is safer a few years from now. I also note that her own first choice, B051, is a real instrument invention. I see it as outside the top group on breadth of physics impact, though I would defend it as an alternative to colleagues who weigh technique heavily.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks Car-Parrinello B043 first as a conceptually clear, four-decade method with overwhelming impact across condensed matter, chemistry and materials, while flagging overlap with the 1998 chemistry prize for DFT.
responses.response: I respect the impact, and I rely on him for condensed-matter judgement. My reservation is the one he names himself: this is a computational method that follows the 1998 DFT prize, and the Physics prize has usually required a discovery or an invention that opens a new observational or experimental capability. Only he supports it, and I do not see it displacing B005 unless the committee decides a method can be the physical advance. I would like to hear how he separates the new physics from the extension of an already honoured framework.

responses.point: Johansson ranks optical-lattice quantum simulation B015 first but also ranks B005 second, and asks whether the committee should wait for the SI second redefinition as a marker of impact.
responses.response: I do not think the committee should wait for the redefinition. The science is already confirmed independently, and the Nobel recognises the invention and its performance, not a metrology-body decision. On B015 I disagree with his first place for a practical reason: four credited names compete for three seats, and several colleagues say that the Zoller, Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger split is genuinely contestable. B005 does not have that attribution problem, and he himself rates its two-person credit as clean.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is distinct enough from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Priority between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and parallel optical-lattice clock ideas, and whether Takamoto, Ludlow or others have claims I cannot assess from the supplied text.

Whether the IceCube source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) and the Galactic plane result are firm enough, and how to credit the work fairly inside a large collaboration, for the case that B035 returns as an alternative.
Whether a two-part prize combining B005 with a single credited name from B035 is acceptable, which seems unfair to Karle and Spiering.
statement.conflict_note: My profile lists membership in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations and a research field (astroparticle physics, space and balloon instruments) adjacent to IceCube, which is my opening first choice and one of my alternatives. I am not an IceCube member and the profile shows no direct connection to its credited names, but I flag the field proximity for the committee. No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile regarding B005 (Katori, Ye) or the other shortlisted candidates.
